steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A spirometer is a device that measures the volume of air inspired and expired by the lungs. It produces a graph (spirometer trace) showing the volume of air breathed over time.

steps.title: Tidal Volume (TV)
steps.body: The volume of air breathed in or out per breath at rest. Approximately 500 ml for an average adult.

steps.title: Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)
steps.body: The additional volume of air that can be forcibly inhaled after a normal tidal inspiration. Approximately 2,500-3,000 ml .

steps.title: Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV)
steps.body: The additional volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled after a normal tidal expiration. Approximately 1,000-1,500 ml .

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Define tidal volume and state its approximate value at rest. | What is the difference between inspiratory reserve volume and expiratory reserve volume? | Calculate vital capacity given: TV = 500 ml, IRV = 3,000 ml, ERV = 1,200 ml.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Tidal volume is the volume of air breathed in or out per breath during normal resting breathing. Its approximate value is 500 ml. | Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) is the extra air that can be forcibly inhaled after a normal tidal inspiration (~3,000 ml). Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) is the extra air that can be forcibly exhal | VC = TV + IRV + ERV = 500 + 3,000 + 1,200 = 4,700 ml.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Know the definitions and approximate values for all lung volumes The vital capacity formula (VC = TV + IRV + ERV) is frequently tested Residual volume is NEVER included in vital capacity calculations When describing spirometer traces, mention both height/amplitude AND frequency Practise minute ventilation calculations (TV × breathing rate) Remember: residual volume does NOT change during exercise or with training
